migrationNotes: Spine: we follow Newton from an apple and the Moon to a single law, adding distance, then the two masses, then dividing out the falling mass to reach g.
Questions astro-newton-gravity-10, astro-newton-gravity-4, astro-newton-gravity-8 are no longer in the lesson; their ids and keys are unchanged in the question bank.

lesson.title: Newton's gravitation

steps.headline: From the apple to the Moon

lead.text: Newton’s idea was that gravity weakens with distance, and the odd number from the opening tells us by how much. The Moon is about 60 times as far from Earth’s centre as the apple is. Square 60 and you get 3,600. If the pull falls as the square of the distance, then at 60 times the distance it is 60 × 60 = 3,600 times weaker, which is exactly the drop in the Moon’s fall.
This is called an inverse-square law. Double the distance and the pull falls to a quarter, because 2 × 2 = 4. Triple it and the pull falls to a ninth.

afterFigure.text: Newton did not take this from theory alone. It is the one rule that fits the falling apple, the Moon and the planets together. The arrows in the drawing share a single scale, so you can watch the force shrink as the two bodies move apart.

lead.text: Apply the same rule to two bodies that are pulled three times as far apart.

reveal.text: You tripled the separation, so the pull fell by 3 × 3 = 9. Gravity follows the square of the distance.

lead.text: Distance is only part of the story, because gravity also depends on how much matter is doing the pulling. Double the mass of the body that pulls and the force doubles. Double the mass of the body being pulled and the force doubles again, which is why a heavier person weighs more. The force depends on the product of the two masses.

Call the masses M and m, and the distance between their centres r. Newton’s law is F = GMm/r². G is the gravitational constant, 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², a fixed number that sets the scale. It is so small that you feel the pull of a whole planet but not of the person beside you.

afterFigure.text: One more fact comes with the law. The pull is shared: when Earth pulls on the Moon with a force F, the Moon pulls back on Earth with exactly the same force, in the opposite direction. The Moon is far more affected because a given force changes the motion of a light body much more than that of a heavy one.

steps.headline: By what factor does the force change when r is halved and one mass is doubled?

workedSteps.text: Halving r multiplies the force by the square of 2.
Doubling one mass multiplies the force by 2.
Each change acts on its own, so the factors multiply.

lead.text: Here the separation stays fixed. Only the masses change.

reveal.text: Each mass scales the pull on its own, so you multiplied the two factors.

steps.headline: What the pull does to a falling object

lead.text: Now apply the law to something falling. The pull on a mass m near a body of mass M is GMm/r². How fast the object speeds up depends on that pull divided by its own mass, because a heavier object needs a bigger push to change its motion by the same amount. Divide by m and the m cancels: g = GM/r².

The result g is an acceleration, the amount by which the object’s speed grows each second. It is called the gravitational field of the body at that place, and 9.8 m/s² would mean a falling object is 9.8 m/s faster after every second.

afterFigure.text: M is the mass of the body doing the pulling (Earth, for example) and r is the distance from its centre. Because the falling object’s own mass has dropped out, every object at that place gets the same acceleration, whatever its weight.

lead.text: At the surface of a world, r is the world’s radius, so g = GM/R². Each world has its own GM, the product of G and its mass. The units matter: GM is in m³/s², so the radius has to be in metres.

Take the Moon, with GM = 4.90 × 10¹² m³/s² and a radius of 1,737 km, which is 1.737 × 10⁶ m. The radius squared is 3.017 × 10¹² m², and dividing GM by it gives g = 1.62 m/s². That is far weaker than the pull you feel on Earth.

afterFigure.text: Two things set the surface gravity of a world. More mass raises it, and a larger radius lowers it, by the square, because the surface is then farther from the centre. A small world can have weak gravity even when it is dense, and a large world can have strong gravity even when it is light.

lead.text: Use SI units. GM is in m³/s², so convert the radius from kilometres to metres before you square it.

reveal.text: That is how fast any object gains speed near Earth’s surface. The same formula gave the Moon’s value from its own GM and radius.

lead.text: The field g = GM/r² applies to any planet. Take a planet with Earth’s mass but twice Earth’s radius.

reveal.text: Doubling r with the mass fixed divides g by four. The same inverse-square rule governs the Moon’s fall and a planet’s surface.

lesson.orientation: Use the inverse-square law of gravity to compare forces and compute surface gravity.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Isaac Newton is said to have been sitting in a garden when an apple dropped from a tree. Whether or not it happened that way, the thought he took from it was that Earth’s pull might not stop at the treetops. It might reach all the way to the Moon, and be the very thing that keeps the Moon from flying off in a straight line.

The numbers pointed that way. An apple drops about 5 m in its first second. The Moon is falling too, in its own fashion: without Earth’s pull it would sail off in a straight line, and each second it drops about 1.4 mm below that line. The Moon is about 60 times as far from Earth’s centre as the apple is, yet its fall is not 60 times smaller. It is about 3,600 times smaller.

That odd number turned out to be the key. This lesson follows Newton from it to a law that covers every pair of masses in the universe, and then uses the law to find how strongly gravity pulls on Earth and on other worlds.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll use F = GMm/r² to say how gravity changes with distance and mass, and to find g.

recap.keyIdea: Gravity pulls every pair of masses with F = GMm/r². The force falls as the square of the separation, and g = GM/r² is the same for every falling object.

blocks.text: You began with the gap between the apple’s fall and the Moon’s, and saw that 60² = 3,600 accounts for it. You found that tripling the separation cuts the pull to a ninth, and that at Earth’s surface g is 9.82 m/s².

recap.nextHook: One law covers the falling apple and the Moon. The next lesson asks how fast something must be thrown to stay in orbit, and how fast to leave Earth altogether.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 3r. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change? Give three decimal places.
hints: Gravity follows an inverse-square law.
Square the factor by which the distance grew.
Take the reciprocal of 3².
questions.onCorrect: 0.111. Force follows 1/r², so tripling the separation divides the force by nine.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the force as falling in proportion to the distance. Gravity follows the square of it.
That makes the force grow. The force weakens as the bodies move apart.

questions.prompt: At a fixed separation, one mass is doubled and the other tripled. By what factor does the gravitational force change?
hints: The force is proportional to the product of the masses.
Each mass change multiplies the force.
Multiply the two factors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F ∝ Mm, so the force changes by 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Force is proportional to the product of the masses, so the factors multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the factors. The force depends on the product of the masses, so the factors multiply.

questions.prompt: Earth's GM is 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and its radius is 6,371 km. Find g = GM/R² at the surface, in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Convert the radius to metres first.
Square 6.371 × 10⁶ m.
Divide GM by that square.
questions.onCorrect: 9.82 m/s². Surface gravity is GM divided by the radius squared, in metres.

misconceptions.feedback: The radius must be in metres to match GM. In kilometres the answer comes out a million times too large.

questions.prompt: How many times as large as the Moon's pull on Earth is Earth's pull on the Moon?
hints: Think of the pair as a tug of war between two bodies.
Whatever force acts on one body from the other, the other feels a force from it.
Newton's third law pairs the two forces.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both forces equal GMm/r², so the ratio is exactly one: equal and opposite.

questions.onCorrect: 1. The two forces are an equal and opposite pair: GMm/r² is the same whichever body you call M.

misconceptions.feedback: The 81 shows up in how much each body accelerates, not in the size of the pull. Think of the pair as one tug of war.

questions.prompt: Mars has GM = 4.283 × 10¹³ m³/s² and radius 3,390 km. Find its surface gravity in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Use g = GM/R² with R in metres.
Square 3.39 × 10⁶.
Divide GM by that square.
questions.onCorrect: 3.73 m/s². The same formula gives each world's surface gravity from its own GM and radius.

misconceptions.feedback: The radius must be in metres to match GM. Kilometres give an answer a million times too large.

questions.prompt: Why do a hammer and a feather dropped together on the Moon land together?
hints: Divide the gravitational force by the falling object's own mass.

acceptedIdeas: The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Force GMm/r² divided by the object's mass m leaves GM/r², the same for any object at that place. With no air there is no drag to separate them.

choices.label: The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
The Moon's gravity does not act on light objects
Heavier objects are pulled less strongly per kilogram

questions.onCorrect: The mass cancels in GMm/r² ÷ m, leaving GM/r². The acceleration is the same for every object.

misconceptions.feedback: Gravity acts on light and heavy objects alike. The question is what it does to their acceleration.
Divide GMm/r² by m and see whether any of the object's own mass is left.

questions.prompt: A planet has Earth's mass but twice Earth's radius. By what factor does its surface gravity change compared with Earth's?
hints: Surface gravity is g = GM/r², and M is unchanged.
Doubling r changes g by the inverse square.
Square the 2, then take the reciprocal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: g = GM/r², so doubling r divides g by 2² = 4, a factor of 0.25.

questions.onCorrect: 0.25. With the mass fixed, g falls as 1/r², so doubling the radius divides it by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves g, as if gravity fell in proportion to the distance. It follows the square.
That makes g larger. A larger radius puts the surface farther from the centre, which weakens the pull.

questions.prompt: Which change weakens the gravitational force between two masses?
hints: Look at where r sits in the formula.
questions.onCorrect: Force grows with the masses and falls as r² grows, so more separation weakens it.

misconceptions.feedback: A heavier mass increases the product Mm, which strengthens the pull.
G is a fixed constant. We cannot change it.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the factors?
hints: In F = GMm/r², how are the quantities combined?

acceptedIdeas: Each change scales the force on its own, so the effects multiply.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each change scales the force on its own, so the effects multiply.

choices.label: Each change scales the force on its own, so the effects multiply.
Because the formula adds the masses.
Because force is the sum of two terms.

questions.onCorrect: The force is a product and a quotient, so separate changes multiply together.

misconceptions.feedback: The formula multiplies the masses, it does not add them.
F is built from a product and a quotient, not a sum.

questions.prompt: In g = GM/r², what does M stand for?
hints: Which mass cancelled when we divided by m?

acceptedIdeas: The mass of the body doing the pulling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mass of the body doing the pulling

choices.label: The mass of the body doing the pulling
The mass of the falling object

questions.onCorrect: M belongs to the body whose gravity we are measuring, such as Earth. The falling mass has cancelled.

misconceptions.feedback: The falling mass is m, and it cancelled when we divided by it.
The Sun is just one possible pulling body. M is whichever body's gravity you are measuring.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 4r. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change? Give four decimal places.
hints: Gravity follows an inverse-square law.
Square the factor by which the distance grew.
Take the reciprocal of 4².
questions.onCorrect: 0.0625. Four times the separation divides the force by 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 4. The force follows the inverse square, so the 4 is squared first.
That makes the force grow. It weakens as the bodies move apart.
